title: The last two classes — and the whole possessive system in one table
goal: Finish the six noun classes with the m-/mi- class and the u- class, then see Swahili's entire system of possessives and linkers on a single page.
bekal: the m-/mi- class: *mti → miti*, subject prefixes *u-* and *i-*
the u- class: *ukuta → kuta*, and idea words like *uhuru*, *upendo*
the complete *-angu/-ako/-ake* table and the linker *-a* for all six classes

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kijijini kwao
dialogs.intro: A weekend in Amina's home village, at the foot of the mountains.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Karibu kijijini kwetu! Huu ni mji mdogo sana.
lines.id: Welcome to our village! It's a very small town.
lines.literal: welcome at-village of-us! this is town small very.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ni mzuri sana. Na miti hii ni mikubwa!
lines.id: It's lovely. And these trees are huge!
lines.literal: is beautiful very. and trees these are big-big!

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Ni miembe. Mwaka huu imezaa sana.
lines.id: That's a mango tree. This year it's full of fruit.
lines.literal: is tree-mango. year this they-have-borne very.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Na mlima ule? Jina lake nani?
lines.id: And that mountain? What's it called?
lines.literal: and mountain that? name of-it who?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Ni Mlima Uluguru. Mto wetu unatoka huko.
lines.id: That's Mount Uluguru. Our river comes from there.
lines.literal: is Mount Uluguru. river of-us it-is-coming from-there.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Safi kabisa. Watoto huogelea humo kila jioni.
lines.id: Very clean. The children swim there every evening.
lines.literal: clean completely. children usually-swim in-it every evening.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Pale, nyuma ya ukuta mweupe. Nina ufunguo wake.
lines.id: Over there, behind the white wall. I have the key.
lines.literal: over-there, behind of wall white. I-have key of-it.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ninasikia muziki. Nyimbo hizi ni za nani?
lines.id: I hear music. Whose songs are these?
lines.literal: I-am-hearing music. songs these are of whom?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Ni za bibi yangu. Anapenda nyimbo za zamani.
lines.id: My grandmother's. She likes old songs.
lines.literal: are of grandmother of-me. she-is-liking songs of long-ago.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ninafurahi kuwa hapa. Ukarimu wenu ni mkubwa.
lines.id: I'm so happy to be here. Your hospitality is huge.
lines.literal: I-am-glad to-be here. hospitality of-you(pl) is big.

notes: **Kijiji means village and kijijini means in the village.** It belongs to the *ki-/vi-* class from unit 6, and its origin is neat: *mji* (town) shrunk with the prefix *ki-* becomes "little town". Swahili builds words from parts it already has, and once you know the parts, the meaning can be guessed.

**Huogelea is the habitual hu- form** you saw in the table in unit 13: no subject prefix at all, meaning "usually swims". It's used constantly to describe what people in a place habitually do: *Watu hapa hulima* (people here farm).

**Humo means "in there".** A cousin of *hapa* (here) and *huko* (there), but specifically for the inside of something — a river, a room, a bag. It's the ending *-mo* you met in *yumo ndani* in unit 8.

**Kuzaa means both to give birth and to bear fruit.** *Mti umezaa* (the tree has borne fruit), *Amezaa mtoto* (she has given birth to a child). The same verb gives *mzazi* (parent) and *uzazi* (birth).

**Ukarimu means hospitality, from karim "generous".** It's a *u-* class word — the class of ideas, where Swahili puts almost all its abstract nouns, just as English uses endings like *-ness*, *-ship* and *-dom*.

grammars.title: The m-/mi- class: trees, long things, and time
body: From the outside this class looks like the people class — its singular also starts with **m-** — but its plural is **mi-**, and its subject prefixes are completely different. It holds plants, long objects, paired body parts, and units of time.
after: Its subject prefixes: **u-** for one, **i-** for many. Its possessives are **wangu / yangu**, its linkers **wa / ya**, its demonstratives **huu / hii** and **ule / ile**.

How to tell it apart from the people class in practice: if the thing isn't a human being, it's almost certainly this class. *Mtoto anakuja* (a person → *a-*) versus *mti unakua* (not a person → *u-*).
⚠️ A small trap: *mto* means both **river** and **pillow**. Context sorts it out, and locals joke about it too.

grammars.title: Possessives and the linker -a: all six classes at once
body: This page is the backbone of Swahili. A possessive is always **the stem -angu/-ako/-ake/-etu/-enu/-ao** with its class prefix in front; the linker *-a* works with exactly the same prefixes.
after: The six possessive stems never change: **-angu** (my), **-ako** (your), **-ake** (his/her), **-etu** (our), **-enu** (your, pl.), **-ao** (their). Only the prefix changes. So *kitabu changu*, *vitabu vyangu*, *nyumba yangu*, *nyumba zangu*, *gari langu*, *magari yangu* — six forms, one stem.

The linker *-a* covers every relationship of "of, belonging to, kind of, for": *mwalimu wa Kiswahili* (Swahili teacher), *kitabu cha Amina* (Amina's book), *maji ya matunda* (fruit juice), *gari la baba* (Dad's car), *nyimbo za zamani* (old songs).

Two possessives that often cause doubt: *-ake* means "his/her" for one owner, while *-ao* means "their". *Nyumba yake* (his/her house) versus *nyumba yao* (their house). Note that the prefix is set by **the thing owned**, not by the owner.

sections.title: The u- class: where Swahili keeps its ideas

blocks.text: The prefix **u-** builds abstract nouns from adjectives or verbs — the very job of English *-ness*, *-ship*, and *-dom*. Once you know the root, you can guess the new word yourself.

The same class also holds thin, long things, and these have a plural: *ukuta* → *kuta* (wall), *ufunguo* → *funguo* (key), *uso* → *nyuso* (face), *wimbo* → *nyimbo* (song), *ubao* → *mbao* (board). Its subject prefixes are *u-* for one and *zi-* for many.

*Uhuru* may be the most famous Swahili word after *safari* and *hakuna matata* — it names streets, stadiums, and monuments across East Africa, and was a keyword of the independence movements of the 1960s. *Uhuru na umoja* (freedom and unity) is Tanzania's national motto.

⚠️ *Maziwa* means both **lakes** and **milk** — two different words whose plural forms happen to match. East Africa's great lakes are called *Maziwa Makuu*, and the biggest, Lake Victoria, is *Ziwa Nyanza* in the local language.

Africa's highest mountain is in Tanzania: *Mlima Kilimanjaro*. The origin of the name itself is debated, but *kilima* in Swahili means "hill" — a diminutive of *mlima*, with the same *ki-* as *kijiji* from *mji*. Read at face value, it's a name meaning "little hill" for a mountain 5,895 meters high.
